AIChipBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for
Automated AI Accelerator Design

Guangyuan Wang1, 2 Chengran Li Minchen Luo3 Jichen Feng4, 5
Mengdi Wang4 †\dagger Yifan Zhang4 †\dagger
1Mila 2McGill University 3Erised Labs
4Princeton University 5University of Pennsylvania
Abstract

A language-model decoder carries state between decoding steps, and in hardware a wrong state update can leave the current token correct and corrupt the output several tokens later, so a design can pass output tests and still be wrong. AIChipBench asks what LLM coding agents need to build such hardware correctly. Agents implement quantized Qwen3.5, Gemma 3, Gemma 4, and Llama 3.2 decoders in synthesizable register-transfer-level (RTL) code against an executable integer reference that specifies the outputs and the stored state at every decoding step. They debug against public tests under fixed budgets; their frozen designs are graded on held-out token sequences, resets, memory stalls, and synthesis, and a second track asks them to speed up a correct design at nearly fixed area. Across 9,136 attempts by four coding agents, the difficulty lies in stored state. Feedback that points to the first state mismatch raises acceptance over output-only feedback in all 12 agent–task cells of a matched study, by 25.0 to 46.9 percentage points, and halves the agent-hours per accepted design. Regraded on new sequences and conditions, 45 of 69 accepted designs fail within the 32 steps their tests required. More than a third of attempts to speed up a correct design end without one. An overall score ranks Sol 5.6 and Fable 5.1 above Astra 6 and Opus 5.5, and both halves of the instances give this order in all 200 random splits. Hardware agents therefore need debugging feedback that exposes stored state, and their benchmarks need final tests well beyond the development cases.

1 Introduction

LLM coding agents now edit hardware code and run the compilers, simulators, and synthesis tools that check it. We study them on one such task, building an accelerator for a language-model decoder. At each decoding step, a decoder reads one token, computes scores over its vocabulary (logits), and updates values that later steps reuse, such as the attention key–value cache and the recurrent states of hybrid layers. This persistent state makes errors easy to miss. Suppose a hardware cache saves a result before the next module has taken it. If that module is busy for a few clock cycles, the cache saves the same result again and now holds an entry that should not exist. The token produced at that step is still correct, and the error reaches the output only when a later step reads the cache. In a small decoder we constructed with this defect, the stored state is first wrong at transaction 2, the logits at transaction 5, and the selected token at transaction 6 (Appendix B.5). A test that compares output tokens over the first few steps passes this design.

We ask what an agent needs in order to get such state right, and how an evaluator can tell whether it did. Two requirements follow. An agent working within a fixed budget needs feedback that points to the faulty update, because an output mismatch several steps later says little about where the error began. The final verdict must also come from tests the agent never saw, because an agent can fit its design to the tests it debugs against. In our runs, 148 agent-built designs pass every public test and fail final acceptance, and when frozen submissions are regraded, 45 of 69 accepted designs fail a new sequence or condition within the 32 steps their tests required.

AIChipBench (Figure 1) is built around these requirements and has three components. The LLM coding agent is a language model run in a tool-using harness: it inspects files, writes and revises hardware code, runs lint, simulation, and synthesis, reads test feedback, and submits a design within caps on wall time, tool calls, and output tokens. The target, a quantized Qwen3.5, Gemma 3, Gemma 4, or Llama 3.2 decoder, defines what the hardware must compute. The integer oracle, an executable reference that fixes every arithmetic decision of the target, gives the exact outputs and the exact stored state expected at each transaction, the point at which the hardware accepts a transfer and commits its result. Agents write register-transfer-level (RTL) code, which describes what a circuit computes and stores on each clock cycle. Synthesis maps that code onto the resources of a chip, here a field-programmable gate array (FPGA), whose logic and wiring are configured after manufacture. A submitted design is frozen and accepted only if it matches the oracle on held-out sequences, resets, and memory stalls, synthesizes, and leaves protected files intact. A second track, on power, performance, and area (PPA), starts the agent from a correct design and asks it to raise throughput by at least 5% with at most 2% more area while every check still passes. In the chip-design flow, which runs from architecture through RTL, verification, synthesis, and placement and routing to fabrication, the agents work at the RTL stage; their designs are placed and routed afterwards for measurement (Section 5).

We evaluate coding agents, which edit, test, and revise over many tool calls, because building a decoder is a multi-step engineering task. A decoder takes thousands of lines of RTL (6,843 to 31,884 in the seven reference designs of the correctness track), and one clean validation-and-synthesis pass on the 0.8B reference takes 162 minutes, so an attempt’s outcome depends on how the agent edits, tests, and spends its budget as well as on the underlying model. This regime differs from single-shot RTL generation, and its results describe a model and its harness together.

Earlier benchmarks cover parts of this setting. CVDP grades tool-using agents that work in a repository against hidden test harnesses, ChipBench includes hierarchical designs and debugging with simulation waveforms, and Build-A-Chip-Bench follows agents from a workload specification to a routed layout (Section 5). AIChipBench adds two capabilities aimed at stateful accelerators: an oracle that specifies the committed state of a decoder at every transaction, and a matched study that varies what public feedback reveals (output mismatches only, a flag that state differs, or the first state word that differs) while submissions are frozen and graded independently. Repeated attempts under fixed budgets measure each agent’s reliability and cost, both when building a correct design and, on the PPA track, when optimizing one, with place-and-route and board measurements.

Four coding agents make 9,136 attempts, and three results stand out. First, what an agent is told about state largely determines whether it succeeds. Feedback that locates the first state mismatch raises acceptance over output-only feedback in all 12 agent–task cells of a matched study, by 25.0 to 46.9 points, and lowers the agent-hours per accepted design from 13.4 to 6.5. It also beats a flag that only reports a state mismatch in all 12 cells, by 9.4 to 37.5 points, so locating the mismatch helps beyond reporting that state differs (Section 4.2). Second, passing a test suite does not establish that a design is exact, and output checks in particular miss errors of state. When 144 frozen submissions are regraded, 17 of the 85 sequences that fail within the required 32 steps are wrong only in stored state, so an output check of that length passes them (Section 4.3). Third, correctness is fragile under optimization: more than a third of the attempts to speed up a correct design end without one (Section 4). An overall score that multiplies the two track scores ranks Sol 5.6 and Fable 5.1 above Astra 6 and Opus 5.5 (Figure 2), and in all 200 random splits of the instances into halves, both halves put the same two agents on top.

2 AIChipBench

2.1 Task shape

Each task asks an agent to implement a quantized language-model decoder, from embedding lookup to output projection, in synthesizable RTL (Figure 1). The agent works in a sandboxed copy of a starting workspace, with tools for lint, compilation, simulation, bounded property checks, and synthesis, under caps on wall time, tool calls, and output tokens. An attempt is one fresh agent process in a fresh workspace; it ends when the agent submits or reaches a cap.

What a correct design computes is fixed by the task’s numerical contract, the integer reference of Section 1. For each target we fix the integer arithmetic (bit widths, accumulation order, rounding, saturation, and the lookup tables that approximate nonlinear functions), so that one decoding step is an integer state transition

(zt,st+1)=Fq​(xt,pt,st,W),st=(stGDN,stconv,Kt,Vt,mt),(z_{t},s_{t+1})=F_{q}(x_{t},p_{t},s_{t};W),\qquad s_{t}=(s_{t}^{\rm GDN},s_{t}^{\rm conv},K_{t},V_{t},m_{t}), (1)

from token xtx_{t} at position ptp_{t}, persistent state sts_{t}, and weights WW to logits ztz_{t} and the next state. The state holds the recurrent and convolution state of Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers, attention key and value caches KtK_{t} and VtV_{t}, and valid lengths and control metadata mtm_{t}; the GDN parts are empty for attention-only decoders. Each integer in the state is a state word. The contract runs as an integer oracle outside the agent’s workspace; agents can query it but not read its code (Appendix A.1).

Public tests in the workspace compare the agent’s RTL with the oracle, from single operators and layers up to the full decoder and multi-step decoding. By default, a failed test reports the first mismatching state word: its layer, token, tensor, and index, and the expected and received integers (full-state feedback). Two weaker settings, used in Section 4.2, report output mismatches only (output-only) or report that state mismatched without locating it (coarse-state).

When the agent submits, its RTL is hashed, frozen, and graded on an independent clean copy. A submission is accepted only if it passes every gate:

Y=Iintegrity⋅Ipublic⋅Iheldout⋅Isynth⋅Ilocal.Y=I_{\rm integrity}\cdot I_{\rm public}\cdot I_{\rm heldout}\cdot I_{\rm synth}\cdot I_{\rm local}. (2)

The gates are (i) an integrity check on protected files; (ii) the full public suite, rerun with state checks whatever feedback the agent saw; (iii) a held-out suite with new quantized weights and token sequences, nonzero cache positions, reset after a nonempty token sequence (reset after activity), bounded memory stalls, and parameter reload (Appendix B.1); (iv) synthesis; and (v) for all tasks except the two nano tasks, bounded safety checks on reduced instances of the controller (local checks). Held-out results never return to the agent. On the correctness track, an attempt that ends at a cap is not graded and counts as a failure. Section 4.3 regrades accepted designs under new conditions.

An example task.

One task asks the agent to adapt a supplied accelerator scaffold to the official 24-layer Qwen3.5-0.8B text configuration (Qwen Team, 2026a) (Figure 3). The scaffold is a working parameterized accelerator, so the module structure is given, and the agent writes the RTL that fits it to the target. Every task has a reference design that passes all gates, so the task can be completed. The nano and Gemma 4 E4B references were written by hand and reviewed independently; for the 0.8B and Llama 3.2 3B references, an agent drafted components that an engineer reviewed, edited, and integrated; the 4B reference was derived from a gate-passing submission of a model outside the four evaluated agents, with 70 lines changed in its reset sequencing and parameter-loading wrapper (Appendix A.1). The 0.8B reference decodes 3.999 tokens per second at a 126 MHz clock, and its contract agrees with the 32-bit floating-point (FP32) model on 99.14% of top-1 next-token decisions.

2.2 What AIChipBench stresses

A decoder task combines five demands.

Integer arithmetic to the bit. The contract fixes every rounding and saturation decision. Requantization, for example, rounds to the nearest integer with ties to even and then clips (Appendix B.4), and a design with the wrong rounding mode fails the public tests (Table 14).

State committed only on accepted transfers. A decoding step takes many clock cycles, and modules exchange data through valid/ready handshakes: a transfer happens only in a cycle in which the sender’s data is valid and the receiver is ready, and otherwise the sender must hold its data (backpressure). A state word may change only when the transfer that produces it is accepted; a design that writes state whenever a result is valid can commit a value twice under backpressure (Appendix B.5). Because designs may pipeline or reorder work, correctness is checked at each transaction, one accepted transfer of an input and its result, and the cycle-level timing is left to the design.

State that stays exact across steps and conditions. Later steps read what earlier steps commit, so a state defect can surface late, as in the constructed decoder of Section 1 (Appendix B.5). There, a scripted repair that guards only the cache payload makes every output exact while the state and commit checks still fail. A design must also stay exact when reset after activity, at nonzero cache positions, and when memory responses stall. A test that starts from reset at position zero with an always-ready memory exercises none of these.

Hardware quality without loss of exactness. In the power, performance, and area (PPA) track (Section 2.4), a correct design is the starting point, and the agent must make it faster at nearly fixed area while every correctness check still passes.

Slow tools under a fixed budget. One clean pass of validation and synthesis on the 0.8B reference design takes 162 minutes, 31 of them for synthesis and timing (Appendix B.7), so a 12-hour attempt fits fewer than five such passes.

2.3 Correctness track: tasks and scoring

The correctness track (Table 1) has twelve tasks on seven targets from three model families: Qwen3.5 (Qwen Team, 2026a; Qwen Team, 2026c), Gemma 3 and 4 (Google DeepMind, 2025; Google DeepMind, 2026), and Llama 3.2 (Meta, 2024). Tasks differ in the starting workspace. In construction from interfaces, the workspace supplies module declarations, testbench interfaces, arithmetic components, and supporting files, but no decoder implementation; in scaffold adaptation, it supplies a working accelerator to adapt. Tasks also differ in the decoding horizon, the number of decoding steps the tests require. Two tasks use Qwen3.5-nano, our name for a compact Qwen-derived configuration with four layers (three GDN, one full attention), width 256, and a 4,096-token vocabulary (Appendix C.1): T2 decodes one step and T3 eight recurrent steps. The labels follow an earlier task series in which T1 is a single decoder layer (Appendix G). The other ten tasks require 32 steps. Across the twelve tasks, reference designs have 6,843 to 31,884 lines of RTL. A scaffold supplies 16,308 to 27,492 of them, and accepted adaptations add a median of 1,382 to 2,311 lines; from interfaces, the agent starts with 284 to 746 lines and accepted designs add a median of 6,154 to 34,300 (Appendix Table 9).

A target qualifies when its reference RTL passes every gate and its contract agrees with the FP32 model on at least 99% of pooled top-1 next-token decisions over common prefixes, a threshold set by this benchmark. The two conditions are distinct. Exactness is whether RTL reproduces the contract, and it is what agents are graded on. Fidelity is how closely the contract approximates the floating-point model; it is a property of the workload, and either can hold without the other (Section 3.3). Qwen3.5-nano falls below the fidelity threshold at 97.22%; we keep it because its tasks measure exactness and its small size keeps repeated attempts affordable. The Gemma 3 4B (text) and Llama 3.2-1B references qualify: each passes all 1,600 public and 240 held-out cases of its 32-step suite, and their contracts agree with FP32 on 99.00% and 99.31% of decisions; both also meet timing (Tables 4 and 70).

On this track we report an agent’s acceptance rate over all attempts, p^=∑iYi/N\hat{p}=\sum_{i}Y_{i}/N, with a Wilson 95% interval. We also report agent-hours per accepted design: total agent time, failed attempts included, divided by the number accepted (Appendix A.3). Two diagnostic studies extend the track: a feedback study repeats three tasks under weaker feedback (Section 4.2), and a controlled matrix varies the horizon, an added state condition, and the budget from one nano scaffold (Section 4.4). Appendix G covers the earlier task series, run by two cohorts at different times.

2.4 PPA track

The PPA track measures hardware quality on four targets: Qwen3.5-0.8B and 4B, Gemma 4 E4B, and Llama 3.2 3B. Every design targets an AMD Alveo U250 FPGA (xcu250-figd2104-2L-e) and is evaluated at a 126 MHz target clock, batch size one, an eight-token prompt, and a common memory-service model. Throughput is R=f/CR=f/C for clock frequency ff, where CC counts all elapsed cycles per decoded token, memory stalls included; area is the FPGA look-up-table (LUT) count LL; power PP covers the FPGA and attached DRAM and excludes the host; and energy per token is P/RP/R. An agent starts from the correct reference design and is asked to improve its throughput, resources, or energy efficiency. Attempt ii counts as improved only if the design stays correct, gains at least 5% throughput, and grows its LUT count by at most 2%:

Si=Iicorrect⋅I[Ri/R0−1≥0.05]⋅I[Li/L0−1≤0.02],S_{i}=I^{\rm correct}_{i}\cdot I\!\left[R_{i}/R_{0}-1\geq 0.05\right]\cdot I\!\left[L_{i}/L_{0}-1\leq 0.02\right], (3)

where R0R_{0} and L0L_{0} are the evaluator’s values for the starting design: 3.999 tokens/s and 61.8k LUTs for 0.8B, 0.800 tokens/s and 69.0k LUTs for 4B, 0.940 tokens/s and 74.4k LUTs for Gemma 4 E4B, and 1.120 tokens/s and 66.6k LUTs for Llama 3.2 3B. Energy efficiency is reported but does not enter the criterion. Each agent makes 96 attempts per target. The 0.8B and 4B reference designs are also carried through the backend: we place and route them with three implementation seeds, check timing closure at 126 MHz, and measure power on an FPGA board (Section 3.2). Agent designs are scored on the evaluator’s throughput, LUT, and energy values; as a check, every correct agent design is also placed and routed with three seeds (Section 3.2).

Physical implementation.

The agent edits only the RTL; placement and routing run after it submits. Designs are implemented with Vivado 2024.1, AMD’s placement-and-routing flow for its devices (AMD, 2026b), which maps a synthesized design onto the U250’s fixed look-up tables, block RAM, DSP slices, and programmable interconnect and produces a bitstream. OpenROAD (Ajayi et al., 2019) automates a different setting, ASIC physical design: its flow takes RTL for a chosen process design kit through floorplanning, placement, clock-tree synthesis, and routing to a layout of standard cells and memory macros. Vivado is the implementation flow for the U250, on which a routed design can be run and its power measured on the board; every routed and board result here is an FPGA result. An ASIC version would need a process design kit, cell and memory libraries, and physical verification, and its results would not be comparable with these FPGA numbers (Appendix E.2).

Overall score.

One number summarizes both tracks: Score=100​c¯​q¯\mathrm{Score}=100\,\bar{c}\,\bar{q}, where c¯\bar{c} is the agent’s acceptance rate averaged over the twelve correctness tasks and q¯\bar{q} its rate of improved designs averaged over the four PPA targets, both as fractions. The score is the product of the two track percentages, so it is high only when both are. All agents attempt the same task instances, so the score’s 95% interval is a paired bootstrap over instances (Appendix D.9).

3 Results

We evaluate four coding agents, Sol 5.6, Astra 6, Opus 5.5, and Fable 5.1, all run through the MathCode harness (Team Math-AI, 2026). Each makes 472 attempts on the correctness track and 384 on the PPA track. The four agents receive the same task instances, starting files, instructions, tools, feedback, and caps; a task instance fixes the initial RTL files, quantized parameter arrays, public inputs, and held-out test assignment. The diagnostic studies bring the total to 9,136 attempts (Appendix Table 7).

Overall score.

Fable 5.1 and Sol 5.6 score 25.0 and 24.5, and Astra 6 and Opus 5.5 score 16.8 and 16.5 (Figure 2); the gap comes mostly from the PPA track. To test whether the order depends on which instances are drawn, we split the matched instances of every task into random halves: both halves rank Sol 5.6 and Fable 5.1 above Astra 6 and Opus 5.5 in all 200 splits, against 17% of splits when the agents’ outcomes are permuted within instances (p=0.001p=0.001; Appendix Table 56). Each track and the controlled matrix also yield an order that recurs across halves, though the orders differ (Appendix D.8). Scoring the PPA factor at the clock each design achieves after place and route gives 23.7 for Sol 5.6, 22.8 for Fable 5.1, 14.9 for Astra 6, and 15.6 for Opus 5.5, and all four differences between an agent of the first pair and one of the second stay below 0.05 after a Holm adjustment (Figure 4b, Appendix Table 65).

3.1 Correctness track

Sol 5.6 has 61.2% of its attempts accepted, Opus 5.5 55.9%, Astra 6 49.8%, and Fable 5.1 48.3%, at 23.9 to 31.4 agent-hours per accepted design (Appendix Table 53). On matched instances, Sol 5.6 is ahead of Astra 6 and Fable 5.1, and Opus 5.5 is ahead of Fable 5.1 (Holm-adjusted p≤0.024p\leq 0.024; Appendix D.8). About 26% of attempts end at a cap without submitting. Between 55 and 70% of attempts pass each suite, but only 48 to 61% pass every gate.

3.2 PPA track

Of 1,536 attempts, 965 keep the design correct and 569 also meet Equation 3 (Table 2). Fable 5.1 improves the design in 184 of 384 attempts and Sol 5.6 in 151, against 123 for Astra 6 and 111 for Opus 5.5, a ranking that differs from the correctness track’s (matched test, p<0.001p<0.001). Among improved designs, the median throughput gain per agent is 12.2 to 17.0%; counting every attempt, an improved design costs 24.9 to 43.0 agent-hours. Because the criterion caps LUT growth, these are gains at nearly fixed area; over all correct submissions, gains are smaller and LUT use rises slightly (Table 63). Throughput and LUT counts are also recorded for the accepted Qwen3.5-0.8B designs of an earlier Sol 5.6 and Astra 6 study on the correctness track, which run at 4.225 to 4.527 tokens/s with about 62k LUTs (Appendix G).

Routed agent designs.

We placed and routed every correct PPA design with three seeds, and 925 of the 965 complete all three routes. At the achieved clock, 528 attempts meet Equation 3: 495 of the 569 nominal improvements hold, 74 are lost, and 33 are gained (Figure 4a, Appendix Table 64). Fable 5.1 loses the most, 28, and keeps the most improved designs, 168, against 146 for Sol 5.6. On the twelve tasks of the correctness track, accepted designs stay close to their references: over the 1,016 synthesized designs the median LUT ratio per task is 0.97 to 1.10, and in a routed sample of 144 designs the median throughput per task is 0.77 to 1.02 times the reference’s (Figure 4d, Appendix D.3).

Backend results on the reference designs.

Each reference design has a baseline and an optimized schedule; the optimized one changes buffering, overlap, and scheduling and keeps the arithmetic and memory-service model. It raises throughput by 12.0% and power by about 3.9%, an estimated efficiency gain of 7.8% (Table 57). After place and route with three seeds, every baseline and every optimized 4B implementation closes timing at 126 MHz; the optimized 0.8B design closes on one of three seeds, so its mean operating clock is 125.3 MHz. Post-route and board results give throughput gains of 11.4 to 12.0% and efficiency gains of 7.5 to 8.5% (Table 3). In the cycle model, compute takes 65% of the baseline cycles per token and memory waits 28% (Appendix E.3).Post-route results also cover the nano, Gemma 4 E4B, Llama 3.2 3B, Gemma 3 4B, and Llama 3.2-1B references, and on eight agent designs and three references board power is within −0.6-0.6 to +3.5%+3.5\% of the post-route activity estimate (Figure 4c, Appendix E.2). Board power is read from the U250’s on-board rail sensors (Appendix E.2).

3.3 Reference designs beyond the benchmark targets

To test whether the contract and evaluator carry to decoders outside the benchmark, we built reference designs for the attention-only Gemma 2 2B (Google, 2024) and the 64-layer hybrid Qwen3.6-27B (Qwen Team, 2026b) (Appendix F.1). Table 4 compares them on exactness and fidelity with four references that qualify: Qwen3.5-0.8B and 4B, and the correctness-track targets Gemma 3 4B and Llama 3.2-1B (Section 2.3). Both meet timing (Table 70), and each fails a different criterion. Gemma 2 2B’s RTL matches its contract on every case, but the contract agrees with FP32 on only 98.38% of decisions. Seven of eight alternative integer contracts reach the threshold, and higher precision costs hardware: LUTs rise from 58.4k to 84.1k and throughput falls from 1.48 to 0.90 tokens/s (Appendix F.2). Qwen3.6-27B’s contract meets the threshold, but its RTL fails eight public and ten held-out cases even though every operator and layer check passes, so the defects appear only when layers are integrated. Two later revisions reduce the failures to one or two cases; neither passes every check, so Qwen3.6-27B does not qualify.

4 Findings

Five findings recur across the two tracks and the diagnostic studies (Figure 5).

4.1 Agents adapt a scaffold more reliably than they build a full-size decoder from interfaces

Acceptance depends strongly on the starting workspace (Table 5). Pooled over agents, 47.7 to 78.9% of scaffold-adaptation attempts are accepted. So are 80.5% (T2) and 71.1% (T3) of attempts on the four-layer nano tasks, which start from interfaces. Building a full-size decoder from interfaces succeeds less often: on 26.0% of attempts for Gemma 4 E4B, 32.3% for Llama 3.2 3B, 32.0% for Gemma 3 4B, and 39.5% for Llama 3.2-1B, and no agent exceeds 10 of 24 on either of the first two. On these four targets every agent does better from the scaffold, 408 of 704 attempts against 239, and construction from interfaces costs 46 to 184 agent-hours per accepted design (Appendices D.1 and D.2). On Gemma 3 4B and Llama 3.2-1B, where each agent attempts 64 matched instances from each start, six of the eight paired differences between starts have intervals that exclude zero (Figure 5d). Appendix C.4 lists the steps that turn a decoder into a task.

Agents also differ on single tasks. Opus 5.5 adapts Qwen3.5-4B in 12 of 24 attempts against 20 or 21 for the others, and Astra 6 and Fable 5.1 build Gemma 3 4B from interfaces in 9 and 14 of 64 attempts against 28 and 31 for Opus 5.5 and Sol 5.6; matched tests confirm both differences (Holm-adjusted p=0.015p=0.015 and p<0.001p<0.001; Appendix D.8). Astra 6 builds Gemma 4 E4B from interfaces in 3 of 24. The ranking also changes between experiments: on the controlled matrix of Section 4.4, Fable 5.1 has 445 of 864 attempts accepted and Sol 5.6, first on the correctness track, has 385 (p=0.001p=0.001). Outcomes also vary between attempts on one instance. With three attempts on each of eight Gemma 4 E4B and eight Llama 3.2 3B adaptation instances, the three outcomes disagree in 26 of 64 agent–instance groups (Appendix D.1).

4.2 Agents do much better when told where state diverges

On nano T2, nano T3, and Qwen3.5-0.8B, each agent attempted 32 task instances under each feedback setting; the three attempts on one instance form a matched block. Full-state feedback raises acceptance over output-only feedback in all 12 agent–task cells, by 25.0 to 46.9 points, and every block-bootstrap interval excludes zero (Appendix Table 34). Pooled, 144, 208, and 295 of 384 attempts are accepted under output-only, coarse-state, and full-state feedback, with nearly equal total agent time, so the cost per accepted design falls from 13.4 [11.3, 16.2] to 6.5 [5.9, 7.3] agent-hours, a ratio of 0.49 [0.42, 0.56]. Output-only and full-state feedback differ both in whether state is visible and in whether the mismatch is located. Coarse-state feedback reports a state mismatch without locating it, and full-state feedback exceeds it in all 12 cells, by 9.4 to 37.5 points, with intervals that exclude zero in seven. Removing any one of the 96 matched blocks keeps the pooled ratio between 0.48 and 0.50, and in each of the 12 agent–task cells the interval of the full-state ratio lies below one (Figure 5a, Appendix D.4). Accepted designs also arrive earlier: by half the wall cap, 82 of 384 full-state attempts had submitted a design that was later accepted, against 67 under coarse-state and 52 under output-only feedback (Appendix D.7).

Comparing the two state settings separates finding a state defect from repairing it. Among attempts with a state defect, agents find it slightly more often under full-state feedback, in 151 of 166 after a median of 1.35 agent-hours, than when told only that state disagrees, in 142 of 169 after 1.50 hours. Repair differs more: agents repair the defect in 123 of the 166 under full-state feedback, after a median of 2.69 hours, and in 87 of the 169 under coarse-state feedback, after 3.22 hours (Table 37). On the constructed decoder of Section 2.2, one Sol 5.6 repair under each setting shows what the agent is told. Full-state feedback reports a cache valid count of 4 at transaction 2, where the oracle expects 2; output-only feedback reports logits [12,12,−6,−5][12,12,-6,-5] at transaction 5, where the oracle expects [13,12,−6,−6][13,12,-6,-6]. Both runs make the same one-line change, committing the cache entry only when the output transfer is accepted, and pass the held-out suite (Appendix B.6).

The gain splits between reporting that state disagrees and locating where. Full-state feedback adds 151 pooled acceptances over output-only feedback; 64 arise between output-only and coarse-state feedback and 87 between coarse-state and full-state feedback. Both increments are positive in every cell. Full-state exceeds coarse-state feedback by 9.4 to 37.5 points, with intervals that exclude zero in seven of the 12 cells; for the gain of coarse-state over output-only feedback, the intervals exclude zero in only two cells (Table 35).

4.3 Passing a test suite does not establish exactness

On the correctness track, 148 designs that pass every public test fail final acceptance, 115 of them on the held-out suite: 25 for Sol, 39 for Opus, 33 for Fable, and 51 for Astra. For the 36 such designs on Gemma 4 E4B, Llama 3.2 3B, and Qwen3.5-4B, the grader’s primary diagnoses are 13 integration, 13 state/protocol, and 10 arithmetic (Appendix D.1). The gap between what the agent sees pass and what is accepted is wider under output-only feedback: of 384 output-only attempts, 219 submit a design that passes every check the agent can see, 199 also pass the full public suite, and 144 are accepted.

Accepted designs can also fail under conditions their tests did not cover. We regraded 144 frozen submissions on Qwen3.5-0.8B, Gemma 4 E4B, and Llama 3.2 3B, 69 of which had been accepted, together with the three reference designs. Each design decodes eight new token prefixes under each of four conditions (a new prefix alone, nonzero cache positions, reset after activity, and bounded memory stalls) for up to 256 steps, which gives 32 sequences per design. The references stay exact throughout. Of the 69 accepted submissions, 45 fail at least one sequence within the 32 steps their tests required, although 2,123 of their 2,208 sequences stay exact. The failures concentrate in the conditions that exercise state: of the 85 failing sequences, 29 fail under bounded memory stalls, 28 under reset after activity, 19 at nonzero cache positions, and only 9 on a new prefix alone. At 256 steps, stalls remain the hardest condition, with 60.6 to 69.9% of sequences exact per target against 75.6 to 86.1% on new prefixes alone (Table 44), and only 20 of the 69 are exact on all eight new prefixes alone, and 482 of the 624 failing sequences first diverge in persistent state, a median of four steps before the output does (Figure 5b). Within the required 32 steps, 17 of the 85 failing sequences, and 5 of the 45 failing designs, are wrong in state only, so an output test of that length would pass them. Longer output tests find these defects later: extended to 35 steps, output checks detect 79 sequences and miss 10 that the 32-step state check finds, and at 48 steps they miss none (Figure 5c, Appendix D.6).

Known defects.

On implementations with known defects, the complete evaluator rejects all 12 development defects and 43 of 48 held-out defects (89.6%); the public tests alone reject 3 of the 12 and 3 of the 48. It accepts every repaired counterpart and correct control (Appendices B.2 and B.3).

4.4 Longer horizons lower acceptance, and the budget binds

The controlled matrix starts every attempt from one Qwen3.5-nano scaffold and varies the required decoding steps (1 to 16), an added state condition (none, reset after activity, or bounded memory stalls), and a multiplier on all three caps. At the 1×\times budget, pooled acceptance falls from 252 to 115 of 288 attempts between one and 16 required steps, and with no added condition every agent has fewer attempts accepted at 16 steps than at one (Table 6). A 1.5×\times budget lifts the 16-step result to 169 of 288, but acceptance still falls at each longer horizon. On the Gemma 3 4B and Llama 3.2-1B tasks, the same instances at eight and at 32 required steps have 558 and 475 of 1,024 attempts accepted (Appendix D.2). How an added state condition changes the horizon effect depends on the budget. At 0.5×\times, where at most 1 of 96 attempts per cell is accepted at 16 steps, the interaction is positive because acceptance has little room to fall; at 1×\times it is negative for reset after activity, and the other intervals include zero (Appendix D.5).

The budget binds on the correctness track as well: 489 of 1,888 attempts end at a cap without submitting (322 on wall time, 105 on tool calls, and 62 on output tokens). Under full-state feedback, caps account for about half of the failures that remain: on the three feedback tasks, 43 of the 89 failed full-state attempts end at a cap, and 39 of these 43 had no state defect or had already repaired it. Caps also end 260 of the 465 failed attempts to build a full-size decoder from interfaces.

4.5 Optimization often ends without a correct design

In the PPA track, 571 of 1,536 attempts end without a correct design, 90 to 185 of 384 per agent: 194 submit an incorrect design, and 377 reach a cap with RTL that fails the correctness checks. Every one of these attempts started from a design that passed every gate. In one such attempt (Figure 6b), Sol 5.6 starts from the correct 0.8B design at 3.999 tokens/s and stops at the tool-call cap with a design that fails the correctness checks and runs at 3.803 tokens/s.

5 Related Work

Where AIChipBench sits in chip design.

A digital design passes through several stages: a specification and an architecture; RTL implementation; functional verification; synthesis onto hardware resources; physical implementation, which places and routes the design and analyzes its timing and power; and finally deployment on an FPGA or fabrication as an application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC). Language models have been applied at several of these stages, including RTL generation, verification, EDA scripting, tool orchestration (Liu et al., 2023a; Wu et al., 2024), and the full path from a workload specification to a routed layout (Gunukula et al., 2026). Given a target decoder and a fixed module structure, AIChipBench’s agents write, debug, and optimize RTL; the evaluator runs verification and synthesis, and placement and routing follow submission (Section 2.4). Architecture design and high-level synthesis lie upstream.

Benchmarks.

VerilogEval (Liu et al., 2023b), built from HDLBits (Wong, 2024) problems, RTLLM (Lu et al., 2024) with its 2.0 release (Liu et al., 2024), TuRTLe (Garcia-Gasulla et al., 2025), and RTL-Repo (Allam and Shalan, 2024) ask a model to generate or complete a module or design and simulate it against references; RTLLM and TuRTLe also score synthesis or PPA. ChipBench (Yu et al., 2026) adds hierarchical and CPU-component generation, debugging, and reference-model generation. CVDP (Pinckney et al., 2025) covers design, verification, debugging, and comprehension, and in its agentic tasks an agent works with tools in a repository before hidden harnesses grade the result; LBC-bench (LBC-bench Team, 2025) reports model and agent results on CVDP tasks. Build-A-Chip-Bench (Gunukula et al., 2026), described in a blog post, carries agents through architecture and physical design to an ASIC layout scored on PPA. Appendix Table 75 compares what each benchmark grades. AIChipBench shares executable tools and hidden grading with the agentic benchmarks. Within a fixed module structure, it measures state-exact correctness of decoder accelerators over decoding steps, the effect of what debugging feedback reveals, and each agent’s reliability and cost over repeated budgeted attempts. Benchmark sizes count problems, designs, examples, or tasks, units comparable neither across benchmarks nor with agent attempts (Appendix H). The closest feedback study is ChipBench’s, which gives models a buggy design with or without simulation waveforms (signals and internal state over time); the waveforms improve results for 8 models and lower them for 13. It differs from ours in information and protocol, so the results are not directly comparable. Architect Labs (Architect Labs, 2026) studies RTL generation with verifiable rewards.

Verification across representations.

EDASYTH (Yuen and Hoang, 2026) gates transitions among symbolic calculations, simulation, and circuit artifacts, EEBench (atopile, 2026) evaluates electrical engineering designs through simulation and cost, and the large-circuit-model perspective (Chen et al., 2024) studies learning across specifications, RTL, netlists, and layouts. AIChipBench checks one transition, from a quantized model to RTL, against an executable state-transition contract.

6 Conclusion

AIChipBench tests whether LLM coding agents can build decoder hardware that stays exact, in outputs and committed state, over many decoding steps, and whether they can make a correct design faster without breaking it. Its results locate the difficulty in stored state. When accepted designs fail under conditions their tests did not exercise, most of the failing sequences diverge in state before the output does, and output checks of the required length miss defects that a state check exposes. Agents, in turn, succeed far more often when they can see that state: feedback that locates the first state mismatch doubles pooled acceptance over output-only feedback, after which caps account for about half of the remaining failures. Correctness is also fragile under optimization, since more than a third of attempts to speed up a correct design end without one. An overall score ranks Sol 5.6 and Fable 5.1 above Astra 6 and Opus 5.5, and the order holds across random halves of the instances. Debugging tools for hardware agents should therefore report stored state, and final evaluations should test well beyond the development cases.

Limitations.

Tasks fix the module structure, and agents do not place and route their designs. Graded horizons stop at 32 steps and regrading at 256. Whether feedback on stored state and held-out state conditions helps on other stateful hardware remains to be tested.
