Appendix A Benchmark protocol and attempt records

Two independently versioned objects identify a reported result: a workload contract and an agent configuration. The manifest fields in Table 8 determine which comparison a reported result supports. Table 7 lists the agent and benchmark studies, the conditions each varies, and the sections that report them, and Figure 7 shows the workflow of one attempt.

Arithmetic versions.

The arithmetic digest in Table 8 identifies one version of a numerical contract. A change in precision, a new nonlinear table, or a different accumulation order requires a new arithmetic version, even if next-token agreement improves. The baseline and optimized schedules of a reference design (Section 3.2) share one version: they use the same integer functions, parameter arrays, sequence lengths, and external-memory behavior, and both convert cycles to throughput at 126 MHz. Their RTL may differ in buffering, overlap, and scheduling; approximations and matrix dimensions stay fixed.

A.1 Task configuration and execution records

Starting files and assistance.

The starting workspace sets how much the agent must implement, so it is part of the task definition. For construction from interfaces, it holds the supplied module declarations, testbench interfaces, arithmetic components, and any working RTL; for scaffold adaptation, it also holds the initial accelerator tree and the configuration that tree supports. Agents can query the reference implementation of the numerical contract through the permitted oracle API but cannot read its source. So that a starting workspace can be reproduced, the protocol requires an inventory, taken before the attempt, of every path the agent can read or edit, including any reference implementation it can access. Separate digests identify the public tests, oracle code, arithmetic tables, held-out evaluator assets, and hardware constraints. Within a task, all agents start from the same implementation. A change to the supplied implementation defines a different starting workspace, even when the instruction text is unchanged. Figure 3 summarizes the Qwen3.5-0.8B adaptation task and its reference design in this form.

How much RTL the agent writes.

Table 9 gives, for each of the twelve tasks of the correctness track, the size of the reference design, the RTL in the starting workspace, and how many lines accepted submissions add and delete relative to their starting files. A scaffold supplies 85 to 88% of the reference’s lines, and accepted adaptations add a median of 1,382 to 2,311 lines and delete 729 to 1,262.5. From interfaces, the workspace holds 284 to 746 lines, and accepted designs add a median of 6,154 lines on nano T2 and 34,300 on Gemma 4 E4B; on Gemma 4 E4B and Llama 3.2 3B the median accepted design adds more lines than the reference contains (34,300 against 31,884 and 27,625 against 26,713). The nano tasks share one reference, and T3’s workspace supplies 132 more lines than T2’s.

Reference designs.

Three engineers built the reference designs of all seven correctness-track targets. Table 10 records the five Qwen3.5, Gemma 4, and Llama 3.2 3B references, and Appendix F.1 describes the Gemma 3 4B and Llama 3.2-1B references and their test suites. The nano and Gemma 4 E4B references were written by hand and then reviewed independently. For the 0.8B, Llama 3.2 3B, Gemma 3 4B, and Llama 3.2-1B references, an agent drafted individual components, and the engineer reviewed, edited, and integrated them. The 4B reference was derived from a submission that passed every gate. The build-session records name the agent of the 0.8B, Llama 3.2 3B, and 4B work as anthropic/claude-opus-4-20251020, which is not one of the four evaluated agents, so no evaluated agent starts from its own code. On the 4B submission the engineer changed 70 lines: 47 in the reset sequencing, which now clears state in a fixed order and zeroes the valid count, and 23 in the parameter-loading wrapper, which now aligns bursts and checks weight addresses against their bounds. The arithmetic datapath and the commit protocol are unchanged. The public and held-out suites were written from the integer contract before any reference RTL existed and do not depend on the agent-drafted source. Every reference then passed the same gates as an agent submission (Equation 2).

Agent configuration and attempt records.

An agent configuration covers the model and the execution settings that govern its behavior. The attempt specification requires the model identifier returned by the provider, its revision when available, the complete system and user prompts, the harness revision, reasoning and sampling settings, the context-management policy, stopping criteria, and explicit caps on wall time, tokens, and tool calls. Termination labels separate timeouts from RTL failure categories. Table 11 gives the caps on wall time, tool calls, and output tokens in each study. The benchmark runs use the provider model identifiers openai/gpt-5.6-sol-20261015 (Sol 5.6), openai/astra-6-20260930 (Astra 6), anthropic/claude-opus-5-5-20251101 (Opus 5.5), and anthropic/claude-fable-5-1-20261101 (Fable 5.1). All four models run at their provider’s default reasoning effort, which is medium.

The results of the earlier task series (Appendix G) report the nano construction tasks and the larger scaffold-adaptation task in separate columns because they start from different workspaces: interface files for nano and a supplied scaffold for adaptation. Table 71 gives the task allocation and caps for that series.

A.2 Attempt counts and statistics

Table 12 counts the 9,136 agent attempts by study: 8,984 in the eight studies it lists, which Sections 3 and 4 summarize, and 152 by Sol 5.6 and Astra 6 on the earlier task series and its feedback pilot.

Single acceptance rates carry Wilson 95% intervals. Paired contrasts carry block-bootstrap intervals over matched instances; those of the feedback and state-condition contrasts are computed from the paired attempt records (Appendices D.4 and D.5).

A.3 Acceptance rate and agent-hours per accepted design

For a fixed task and agent configuration, independent attempts yield binary outcomes YiY_{i}, with Yi=1Y_{i}=1 when attempt ii is accepted, and the acceptance rate is p^=∑iYi/N\hat{p}=\sum_{i}Y_{i}/N. The correctness track has 24, 32, or 64 attempts per agent on each task (Table 1). The earlier task series has 16 attempts per agent on each nano task and 12 on 0.8B adaptation; Table 72 reports its counts.

For attempt costs cic_{i}, the cost per accepted design is

c^accepted=∑i=1Nci∑i=1NYi.\widehat{c}_{\rm accepted}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}c_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{i}}. (4)

The numerator keeps the costs of failed attempts, and the ratio is undefined, not zero, when no attempt is accepted. With agent time as the cost, this ratio is the agent-hours per accepted design reported in Table 53. It summarizes the observed attempts; reading it as the expected cost of future retries requires a model of how repeated attempts are distributed. Dividing the median cost by p^\hat{p} generally gives a different value.

Appendix B Tests, evaluator checks, and RTL components

B.1 Public and held-out tests

The public suite shows the agent the interface and gives reproducible feedback. The held-out suite changes seeds and short token sequences and uses only operations the contract supports. Table 13 pairs each kind of public test with its held-out variation. A test case is one complete stimulus and its checks; the tensor elements within a case are not independent statistical trials. One mismatch fails a case, and one failed required case fails the suite’s gate (IpublicI_{\rm public} or IheldoutI_{\rm heldout} in Equation 2). The longest decoding tests run 32 steps.

New weights and inputs.

The held-out suite’s new quantized weights are arrays generated within the supported shapes and ranges; they can catch hard-coded vectors and stale weight buffers. The scales are not randomized, because arbitrary scales would violate the frozen arithmetic contract. Fidelity to FP32 is measured with weights derived from the model checkpoint (Section 3.3).

Fidelity by decoding position.

The pooled fidelity of the Qwen3.5-0.8B and 4B contracts rests on 1,000 sequences at each of eight decoding positions: 7,931 of 8,000 top-1 decisions match FP32 for Qwen3.5-0.8B (99.1375%) and 7,937 for Qwen3.5-4B (99.2125%). Table 67 gives the breakdown by position in percent for all six reference targets. Qwen3.5-nano uses 256 sequences per position and matches FP32 on 1,991 of 2,048 decisions. Both executions see the same token histories, but the FP32 and integer states each evolve under their own arithmetic.

Local checks.

The local checks of Equation 2 are bounded safety checks on reduced instances of the controller. They assume a single clock, reset at the initial step, in-order memory responses, and response stalls of at most three cycles, and they run for 32 cycles. Five properties are checked: the output payload is stable while blocked, one accepted request commits at most once, reset clears valid state, issued addresses are in the configured range, and reload occurs only while idle.

B.2 Development defects

To check that the acceptance gates reject known defects, we grade twelve implementations that each contain one specified defect, together with a correct control. The unit is one known-defect implementation. The control must pass every gate, and each known-defect implementation must be rejected by at least one. Table 14 gives the outcome of every gate.

The public tests reject three of the twelve: incorrect rounding, signed-accumulator truncation, and late convolution-state writeback. The held-out numerical tests reject these three and seven more: saturation, GDN update ordering, cache position, reset leakage, the public-vector hard-code, the held-out group-size hard-code, and fixed memory latency. The remaining two pass both numerical suites; they are a non-synthesizable lookup, which synthesis rejects, and an edit to the protected evaluator, which the integrity gate rejects. Together the numerical, synthesis, and integrity gates reject all twelve and accept the control.

The rejection sets overlap, so their counts cannot be added; the integrity gate, for instance, also rejects the public-vector hard-code. Each of the three kinds of gate rejects at least one defect that the other two accept, which supports keeping all three in the acceptance rule. Protected-file hashing and test isolation address different risks, and the evaluator needs both: hashing detects edits to protected files, and isolation keeps held-out assets out of the agent’s workspace. The held-out defect study (Appendix B.3) measures detection on a broader sample of 48 defects.

The protocol ties any reported first-detection time to an activated defect and an identified stimulus, and it reports a defect that is never activated within the test horizon separately from one that executes and escapes every assertion.

B.3 Held-out defects

The held-out defect study adds 48 defects in eight families to the twelve development defects (Section 4.3). Each of the 48 has a repaired counterpart, and there are eight independent correct controls (Figure 8, Tables 15 and 16). The public tests alone reject 3 of the 48 defects, the two numerical suites together 29, the numerical suites and synthesis 34, and the complete evaluator 43 (89.6%). None of the 56 correct implementations (48 repaired, eight controls) is rejected, so the evaluator separates 43 defect–repair pairs. The five missed defects are one each in wiring/integration, reset/isolation, and synthesis, and two in local properties.

B.4 Arithmetic and state-commit RTL components

This subsection describes two components the main text refers to (Section 2.2): the requantizer (Listing 1) and a buffer that commits state only on accepted transfers. A directed testbench for both covers positive and negative rounding ties, saturation, enqueue without commit, a three-cycle stall, simultaneous pop/push, and reset isolation. Each module is complete at its stated interface.

Nearest-even requantization.

For shift kk, write x=2k​q+rx=2^{k}q+r with 0≤r<2k0\leq r<2^{k} and q=⌊x/2k⌋q=\lfloor x/2^{k}\rfloor. Increment qq when r>2k−1r>2^{k-1}, or on an exact tie when qq is odd; then saturate. This formulation also handles negative ties, because an arithmetic right shift computes the floor quotient. Taking the absolute value first would overflow at the most negative representable input and would need special handling. The module’s legal domain is 1≤SHIFT<IN_W1\leq\texttt{SHIFT}<\texttt{IN\_W} and 2≤OUT_W≤IN_W2\leq\texttt{OUT\_W}\leq\texttt{IN\_W}.

State commit and cancellation.

The one-entry buffer accepts a new pending state word when it is empty or when the current word is consumed, and architectural state changes on output acceptance. A simultaneous pop/push commits the old payload and retains the new one, using nonblocking assignments. Reset or a new-sequence request cancels pending work and clears the state. A system with a different reset policy needs a different contract and different tests.

B.5 Delayed state failure in a constructed attention decoder

This section shows a delayed state failure in a decoder with a cache, handshakes, and a memory interface, small enough to inspect in full. The authors constructed it for this case study: one attention head over a four-token vocabulary, embedding width 2, an eight-entry key–value cache of 16-bit words, 32-bit accumulators, one memory response per token, and valid/ready handshakes on input, memory, and output. A state word is the cache’s valid count or one cache entry. The reference RTL is one module of 143 lines, 134 of which are neither blank nor comment-only, and the testbench has 110 lines (Table 18). An integer oracle computes the expected logits and state. All results in this section come from Icarus Verilog simulation of each snapshot on a fixed, directed public suite of four cases (24 transactions) and a held-out suite of five cases (31 transactions).

The seeded defect writes the cache entry and increments the valid count whenever the output is valid, before the output transfer is accepted. Under output backpressure the design therefore commits one token more than once. In the public case with output stalls, the valid count is first wrong at transaction 2, the logits at transaction 5, and the selected token at transaction 6 (Figure 9). Two scripted repairs follow (Table 17). The first guards the cache payload with the output handshake but still increments the valid count; every logit and token of the public suite is then exact, while the state and commit checks still fail, and the held-out suite still fails four of five cases. The second commits the entry and the count only on an accepted output transfer and passes both suites; it reproduces the reference RTL byte for byte. The authors wrote both repairs as patches and replayed them in order, so the sequence shows what each check reports on a known defect. Appendix B.6 gives an agent run on the same defect, and the regrading of 144 frozen agent submissions and the three references (Section 4.3) is the corresponding evidence from real submissions.

B.6 A paired debugging trace

To show what an agent does with each kind of feedback, Sol 5.6 repaired the seeded decoder once under full-state and once under output-only feedback (Table 19). Both runs start from the same RTL and see the same public suite, which fails one of four cases. Full-state feedback names the first mismatching state word: at transaction 2 the cache’s valid count is 4 where the oracle expects 2. Output-only feedback reports the first output mismatch, the logits of transaction 5. In both runs the agent’s first and only edit changes the commit condition from output valid to output valid and ready, a one-line change; the public suite then passes, the agent submits, and the frozen RTL passes all five held-out cases. On this small defect both settings lead to the same repair, and full-state feedback points to the premature commit three transactions earlier. One run per setting shows the mechanism; the feedback study of Appendix D.4 measures the rates. The runs use temperature 0.2, top-p 0.95, reasoning disabled, a 131,072-token context that keeps every public message without compaction, and caps of 24 tool calls, 0.5 hours, and 25,600 output tokens.

B.7 Failure labels, attempt records, and two case studies

Failure labels.

The grader policy labels a rejected submission by its first failing gate, in the order integrity, compilation, public suite, held-out suite, synthesis, and local checks; an attempt that ends at a cap is not graded. For the case checks of the decoder evaluator, the policy takes the first failing check in a fixed order: input timeout, output timeout, incomplete transactions, reset clearing, output stability under stalls, cache bounds, commit atomicity, state mismatch, logit mismatch, and token mismatch. A label names the category of the first failing check. On the 36 snapshot–case records of the constructed decoder (Appendix B.5), two annotators labeled each record independently; they agree on 28 (Cohen’s κ=0.46\kappa=0.46, 95% interval 0.21 to 0.68), and they agree with the rule on 34 and 28.

Excerpts from attempt records.

Figure 6 gives excerpts from the records of three attempts that fail in different ways: at the wall cap after the state defect was repaired, at the tool-call cap during optimization, and on the frozen RTL after every check the agent could see had passed.

Scaffold-adaptation case studies.

Two stored trajectories, one for Qwen3.5-0.8B and one for Qwen3.5-4B, each document a single accepted scaffold adaptation (Table 20). Acceptance rates come from repeated attempts: for 0.8B, those of the earlier task series (Appendix G), and for 4B, the 96 adaptation attempts of the cross-architecture study (Appendix D.1). The 4B case study is not one of the counted attempts.

A clean pass starts from correct RTL and runs validation and synthesis once each. It takes 162.2 minutes for 0.8B and 225.8 minutes for 4B, of which 31 and 44 minutes are synthesis and timing. Agent time in Table 20 covers the iterative development within one attempt; agent-hours per accepted design (Appendix A.3) also count the time of failed attempts.

Appendix C Benchmark targets

C.1 Qwen3.5-nano

Qwen3.5-nano is our compact Qwen-derived test model. It has four layers (three GDN and one attention layer), hidden width 256, intermediate width 768, and vocabulary 4,096. It is the target of the nano correctness-track tasks (T2 and T3), the controlled matrix, and the earlier task series.

Reference exactness and fidelity.

The nano reference passes all 1,384 public cases. Its contract agrees with FP32 on 1,991 of 2,048 top-1 decisions over common prefixes (97.22%), below the 99% fidelity threshold. During development, the reference moved from 62 of 64 to 64 of 64 exact full-model tests and from 27 of 32 to 32 of 32 exact eight-token sequences, while its operator and single-layer tests stayed exact. The development failures were at integration boundaries, and the arithmetic definition did not change while they were fixed.

Reference hardware.

The nano target is not part of the PPA track, but its reference design has a baseline and an optimized schedule, as the 0.8B and 4B references do (Section 3.2). Table 21 compares the two. The optimized schedule improves throughput by 10.5% and estimated energy efficiency by 7.8%, and energy per token falls from 0.0162 to 0.0150 J.

C.2 Qwen3.5-0.8B and 4B configurations

Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-4B are the targets of two scaffold-adaptation tasks and of the PPA track. Qwen3.5-0.8B has 24 layers, hidden width 1,024, intermediate width 3,584, and vocabulary 248,320; Qwen3.5-4B has 32 layers, hidden width 2,560, intermediate width 9,216, and vocabulary 248,320. Both text configurations include attention output gating, convolution length four, and a full-attention layer every fourth layer.

C.3 Qualification of Gemma 4 E4B and Llama 3.2 3B

Agents attempt only targets whose reference design passes every gate (Section 2.3). Gemma 4 E4B [Google DeepMind, 2026] and Llama 3.2 3B [Meta, 2024] were evaluated under two contract conditions, labeled Main and QF in Table 23. Under the Main contracts, both pass all 1,600 public and 240 held-out cases, synthesis, integrity, and local checks, and their contracts agree with FP32 on 99.78% and 99.76% of 4,096 pooled decisions. Every staged check passes, from operators through 32-step decoding, reset, stalls, and parameter reload (Table 24). Under QF, Gemma 4 E4B falls to 98.49% agreement, and Llama 3.2 3B fails three held-out cases and its local check, so neither target qualifies there. All agent attempts use the Main contracts. For comparison, Table 22 lists the same reference checks for the six targets of Table 4.

C.4 Adding a target

A decoder becomes an agent task after four steps, which the Gemma 3 4B and Llama 3.2-1B tasks of Appendix D.2 also followed. First, an integer contract for the decoder configuration fixes the quantized parameters, every rounding and saturation decision, and the state words the oracle checks after each step (Equation 1). Second, the contract must agree with the FP32 model on at least 99% of top-1 next-token decisions; Gemma 2 2B misses this threshold (98.38%) and is not an agent task, and Gemma 4 E4B misses it under its QF contract (98.49%), so its tasks use the Main contract. Qwen3.5-nano is the one exception: its contract reaches 97.22%, and it is kept because its tasks measure RTL exactness and its small size allows repeated attempts (Section 2.3). Third, a reference design must pass every gate of Equation 2: the public suite, the held-out suite with new weights, prefixes, cache positions, reset after activity, memory stalls, and parameter reload, synthesis, integrity, and the local checks. Qwen3.6-27B’s reference fails eight public and ten held-out cases and is not an agent task. Fourth, the task fixes the starting workspace (interfaces or a scaffold), the required horizon, and the caps, and the agents attempt matched instances. Gemma 3 4B and Llama 3.2-1B passed the first three steps and became four tasks of the correctness track (Section 3.3).

Appendix D Correctness track: detailed results

D.1 Scaffold adaptation and construction from interfaces

Five tasks of the correctness track use Gemma 4 E4B, Llama 3.2 3B, and Qwen3.5-4B: scaffold adaptation on all three targets and construction from interfaces on the first two. We call them the cross-architecture tasks. Each agent makes 24 attempts on each (Table 25, Figure 10, Tables 26–28). On Gemma 4 E4B and Llama 3.2 3B, 116 of 192 scaffold-adaptation attempts are accepted against 56 of 192 from interfaces, and every agent does better from the scaffold on both targets. On Qwen3.5-4B, between 12 of 24 (Opus 5.5) and 21 of 24 (Astra 6 and Fable 5.1) attempts are accepted. Construction from interfaces costs 53.8 to 184.0 agent-hours per accepted design, against 12.2 to 37.6 for adaptation.

Tables 29 and 30 follow all 480 attempts through the gates, by agent. A quarter of the attempts (120 of 480) end without an eligible submission. The public suite rejects 78 of the remaining 360 and the held-out suite 36 more, and every attempt that passes both suites also passes synthesis and the local checks. For the 36 rejected designs that pass the public suite, the grader’s primary diagnosis is integration in 13, state/protocol in 13, and arithmetic in 10.

A separate set of repeated attempts measures how much outcomes vary on one instance. Each agent makes three attempts on each of eight Gemma 4 E4B and eight Llama 3.2 3B adaptation instances, 192 attempts in all, which are not counted in the 24-attempt cells above. Of the 64 agent–instance groups, all three attempts are accepted in 27 and none in 11; in the other 26 (41%), one or two are accepted (Figure 10d).

D.2 Gemma 3 4B and Llama 3.2-1B tasks

Four tasks of the correctness track use Gemma 3 4B (text) and Llama 3.2-1B (Section 2.3), each from a scaffold and from interfaces. They require 32 decoding steps and have 1,600 public and 240 held-out cases each. Each agent makes one attempt per task on each of 64 instances of a target, and the eight attempts on one target instance (four agents, two starts) form a matched block: 1,024 attempts in 128 blocks (Figure 11, Table 32). The two starts carry different caps, 16 to 18 hours, 560 to 600 tool calls, and 340k to 360k output tokens from a scaffold against 28 to 30 hours, 860 to 900 calls, and 560k to 600k tokens from interfaces, so a contrast between starts compares complete protocols.

Pooled over agents, 122 of 256 scaffold attempts are accepted on Gemma 3 4B and 170 on Llama 3.2-1B, against 82 and 101 from interfaces, at 29.0 and 18.2 agent-hours per accepted design from a scaffold against 72.5 and 55.9 from interfaces. Every agent has more attempts accepted from the scaffold on both targets. The paired difference is 6.3 to 45.3 points, and six of the eight intervals exclude zero, three after a Holm adjustment. Caps end 326 of the 1,024 attempts: 205 on wall time, 76 on tool calls, and 45 on output tokens. Sol 5.6 has the most accepted attempts on Gemma 3 4B from interfaces and on Llama 3.2-1B from a scaffold and ties Opus 5.5 on Gemma 3 4B from a scaffold; Astra 6 has the most on Llama 3.2-1B from interfaces. Four of the 24 pairwise agent contrasts stay below 0.05 after a Holm adjustment, three of them on Gemma 3 4B from interfaces, where Astra 6 and Fable 5.1 are accepted on 9 and 14 of 64 instances against 28 and 31 for Opus 5.5 and Sol 5.6.

The same 128 blocks were first run with eight required decoding steps and suites of 1,320 public and 80 held-out cases, under the same caps (1,024 further attempts, Table 31). These runs are kept as a horizon comparison and do not enter the correctness track. Pooled acceptance is 558 of 1,024 at eight steps and 475 at 32. It falls in 14 of the 16 agent–task cells, most for Sol 5.6 from the Gemma 3 4B scaffold (48 to 35 of 64), and rises for Astra 6 on both Llama 3.2-1B tasks. Caps end 263 attempts at eight steps and 326 at 32, and the mean agent time per attempt rises from 12.8 to 17.8 hours.

D.3 Hardware of accepted correctness-track designs

All 1,016 designs accepted on the twelve tasks of the correctness track, the 246 of the cross-architecture tasks, the 295 full-state designs of the feedback study, and the 475 of the Gemma 3 4B and Llama 3.2-1B tasks, were synthesized, and three accepted designs per agent and task, 144 in all, were placed and routed with three seeds each (Figure 12, Table 33). Each ratio divides by a reference at the same implementation stage and workload. At synthesis, the median LUT ratio per task is 0.97 to 1.10. Construction from interfaces gives both the largest ratios, 1.08 on Gemma 4 E4B and 1.10 on Llama 3.2 3B, and the smallest, 0.97 on Gemma 3 4B and 0.98 on Llama 3.2-1B. Of the 432 route runs, 421 complete, and 134 of the 144 designs complete all three. Among complete designs, the median routed throughput per task is 0.77 to 1.02 times the reference’s, lowest from interfaces on Llama 3.2 3B and Gemma 4 E4B (0.77 and 0.81). Between 11 and 33 of each task’s 36 route runs close timing at 126 MHz, fewest on Qwen3.5-4B. Nano throughput uses one transaction from reset.

D.4 Feedback study

In the feedback study, each of the four agents attempts 32 task instances on nano T2, nano T3, and Qwen3.5-0.8B under each of the three feedback settings, and the three attempts on one instance form a matched block (Figure 13, Tables 34, 35, and 36). Full-state feedback raises acceptance over output-only feedback in all 12 agent–task cells, by 25.0 to 46.9 points, and every block-bootstrap interval excludes zero. Pooled, 295, 208, and 144 of 384 attempts are accepted under full-state, coarse-state, and output-only feedback. Total agent time is nearly equal across the settings, about 1,930 agent-hours each, so the cost per accepted design falls from 13.4 agent-hours under output-only feedback to 9.3 under coarse-state and 6.5 under full-state feedback. An earlier comparison with Sol 5.6 alone, on 16 instances each of T2 and T3, points the same way: full-state feedback adds two accepted attempts per task (Appendix G).

Full-state feedback exceeds coarse-state feedback in all 12 cells, by 9.4 to 37.5 points, and these intervals exclude zero in seven of 12 cells; the intervals for coarse-state against output-only feedback exclude zero in two. Intervals are percentile block bootstraps (2,000 resamples of whole blocks, fixed seed), computed from the paired attempt records. Across 100 bootstrap seeds, the full-minus-output intervals exclude zero in all 12 cells under every seed. The full-minus-coarse intervals exclude zero in six to eight cells and the coarse-minus-output intervals in two to four, because several of their bounds lie at zero.

Output-only feedback reports no state values, so whether an agent has found a state defect can be observed only under the other two settings. Among attempts with a state defect, agents found it within budget in 142 of 169 coarse-state attempts and 151 of 166 full-state attempts, and repaired it in 87 and 123 (Table 37). Measured from the start of the attempt, the median discovery took 1.50 agent-hours and 58 tool calls under coarse-state feedback and 1.35 hours and 57 calls under full-state feedback. The median completed repair took 3.22 hours (118 calls, 51.4k output tokens) and 2.69 hours (117 calls, 52.6k tokens).

Uncertainty of the cost per accepted design.

Table 38 adds intervals to the pooled costs. Each bootstrap draw resamples whole matched blocks, which keeps the four agents and three settings of an instance together; failed and capped attempts count toward agent time, and grading time does not. Pooled over agents and tasks, output-only feedback costs 13.38 [11.25, 16.19] agent-hours per accepted design, coarse-state 9.33 [8.16, 10.77], and full-state 6.55 [5.92, 7.31]; as ratios to output-only, 0.70 [0.60, 0.81] and 0.49 [0.42, 0.56]. Per agent and task (Table 39), every full-state ratio has an interval below one, from 0.29 [0.12, 0.50] for Sol 5.6 on T3 to 0.65 [0.44, 0.90] for Opus 5.5 on T2, while eight of the 12 coarse-state intervals include one. To check whether a few attempts drive the ratios, we removed one matched block at a time. Over all 96 deletions the pooled full-state ratio stays between 0.48 and 0.50, and no deletion raises an agent–task full-state ratio above 0.71 (Figure 14). Removing single attempts, over all 1,152 deletions, keeps the pooled ratio between 0.486 and 0.492.

D.5 Controlled horizon, added state condition, and budget

Nano tasks T1 to T3 differ in several properties at once. The controlled matrix instead starts every attempt from one Qwen3.5-nano scaffold, grades it with the same evaluator, and varies three factors: the number of decoding steps that must match (1, 4, 8, or 16), an added state condition (none, reset after activity, or bounded memory stalls), and a budget multiplier that scales all three caps (0.5, 1, or 1.5). The public and held-out suites grow with the horizon, from 984 and 68 cases at one step to 1,344 and 128 at 16. Each agent has 24 blocks per cell (Figure 15, Tables 40–41).

At the 1×\times budget with no added condition, every agent has fewer attempts accepted at 16 steps than at one: Sol 5.6 falls from 21 to 8, Astra 6 from 23 to 15, Opus 5.5 from 21 to 10, and Fable 5.1 from 23 to 17, out of 24. Pooled over agents and added conditions, acceptance at the 1×\times budget falls from 252 to 115 of 288 between one and 16 steps (Table 6). The starting implementation, evaluator, and caps are the same in every cell, so the drop follows from the longer required horizon.

At the 0.5×\times budget, most attempts cannot finish within their caps: 192 of 288 one-step attempts and 286 of 288 sixteen-step attempts end at a cap, and 83 and one are accepted. Table 6 omits this budget for that reason, but the result shows that the 1×\times budget is not slack. At one step, only 8 of 288 attempts reach a cap at the 1×\times budget, and a 1.5×\times budget does not raise acceptance (247 against 252 of 288).

Bounded stalls lower pooled acceptance more than reset after activity at most horizons. Of the 144 per-agent intervals for a single added condition, 16 exclude zero (15 to 18 across 100 bootstrap seeds), against about seven expected under no effect. In 15 of the 16, acceptance is lower with the added condition, mostly stalls.

Horizon by added condition.

Table 42 and Figure 16 ask whether an added state condition changes how acceptance falls with the horizon. For each budget, the horizon effect is acceptance at 16 steps minus acceptance at one step, and the interaction is the horizon effect with an added condition minus the effect without one. At 0.5×\times, both interactions are positive, 15.6 points [5.2, 26.0] for reset after activity and 27.1 [18.8, 35.4] for stalls: at 16 steps, at most 1 of 96 attempts per condition is accepted, so conditions that start lower at one step have less room to fall. At 1×\times, the interaction is −15.6-15.6 [−28.1-28.1, −2.1-2.1] for reset and −8.3-8.3 [−24.0-24.0, 7.3] for stalls, and at 1.5×\times both intervals include zero. The intervals are pointwise and clustered on the 24 shared instances.

D.6 Long-horizon regrading

Section 4.3 reports the regrading of 144 frozen submissions on Qwen3.5-0.8B, Gemma 4 E4B, and Llama 3.2 3B, 12 per agent and target, together with the three reference designs. Figure 17 and Tables 43 and 44 give the results at every horizon. Regrading involves no new attempts and changes no acceptance decision. The 69 accepted submissions are all exact at eight steps. At 32 steps, the horizon their tasks required, 85 of their 2,208 sequences fail, in 45 submissions. On new prefixes alone, 454 of their 552 sequences are still exact at 256 steps. Stalls remain the hardest condition at 256 steps, with 60.6 to 69.9% of sequences exact per target against 75.6 to 86.1% on new prefixes alone (Table 44). Of the 624 sequences that fail at 256 steps, 482 first diverge in persistent state and 142 in output arithmetic. In 470 of the 482, the output also mismatches within 256 steps, a median of four decode positions after the first state mismatch (interquartile range two to eight, at most 40); in the other 12, no output mismatch appears within 256 steps. Counted by design instead of by sequence, 24 of the 69 accepted submissions are exact on all 32 sequences at 32 steps, seven at 64 steps, and none at 128 steps.

Table 45 separates the failing sequences by what is wrong. At the 32 steps the tasks required, 85 sequences of the accepted submissions fail: 51 in both stored state and output, 17 in state only, and 17 in output only. A test of that length that compared outputs alone would pass the 17 state-only sequences, nine of which are under bounded memory stalls and five under reset after activity. Longer runs do not add such sequences: at 256 steps, 12 of the 624 failing sequences are wrong in state only. Counted by design (Table 46), 45 accepted designs fail within 32 steps and 5 of them fail only in state; from 128 steps on, all 69 fail in output. Of the 482 sequences that first diverge in state, 470 show a wrong output a median of four steps later (quartiles 2 and 8, maximum 40), and 12 show none within 256 steps (Figure 18).

Longer output-only checks.

Table 47 compares the 32-step full-state check with output-only checks of 32 to 64 steps on the same 2,208 sequences. The full-state check detects 85 sequences in 45 designs, and the 32-step output check 68 in 40. At 35 steps the output check detects 79 sequences; it still misses 10 that the full-state check finds and finds 4 that it misses, a difference of 0.27 points [−0.05-0.05, 0.63]. From 38 steps on, the output check detects more sequences than the 32-step full-state check, and at 48 steps it detects all 85, among 117 in 53 designs. On these designs, a full-state check finds the defects at a shorter horizon, and an output check that runs 50% longer finds the same ones.

D.7 Submission timing and failure outcomes

Figure 19 and Table 48 classify every attempt in the feedback study, on Gemma 4 E4B and Llama 3.2 3B, and in the controlled matrix at the 1×\times budget by how it ended: accepted, submitted and rejected (with the grader’s primary diagnosis), or stopped at the wall-time, tool-call, or output-token cap. From output-only to full-state feedback, state/protocol rejections fall from 81 to 17 of 384 attempts and cap exits from 58 to 43. Under full-state feedback, caps end 43 of the 89 failed attempts: 26 had no state defect, 13 had already repaired one, and four reached the cap before the repair was complete. Caps also end 70 of the 136 failed attempts at construction from interfaces and 86 of the 173 failed 16-step attempts in the controlled matrix. Figure 6 gives excerpts from three attempt records.

Under every feedback setting, accepted designs were submitted at a median of 56 to 59% of the wall cap, but the settings separate early. By half the cap, 52, 67, and 82 of 384 attempts under output-only, coarse-state, and full-state feedback had submitted a design that was later accepted, and by three quarters of the cap, 122, 164, and 232 had. Only 6, 10, and 20 accepted designs were submitted after 90% of the cap. On Gemma 4 E4B and Llama 3.2 3B, accepted designs arrived at medians of 67% (scaffold adaptation) and 66% (construction from interfaces) of the cap, and 85 and 36 of 192 attempts had submitted one by three quarters of it. The controlled matrix varies the caps directly (Appendix D.5).

Table 50 follows each submission in the feedback study from the checks the agent could see to final acceptance. Under output-only feedback, 219 submissions pass every visible check, 199 pass the full public suite with its state checks, and 144 are accepted. Under coarse-state and full-state feedback, every submission that passes the visible checks also passes the full public suite (252 and 314), and 208 and 295 are accepted.

D.8 Agent comparisons on matched instances

In every experiment the four agents attempt the same instances, so they are compared within an instance. Table 51 tests, for each experiment, whether the agents are interchangeable within an instance, and Table 52 gives the pairwise differences on the correctness track.

Three experiments rank the agents, and their rankings reproduce across random halves of the instances (Table 56). On the correctness track, Sol 5.6 has 289 of 472 attempts accepted, Opus 5.5 264, Astra 6 235, and Fable 5.1 228 (p<0.001p<0.001); the Kendall τ\tau between the orders of two random halves averages 0.78 (p=0.001p=0.001), and the halves give the same order of all four agents in 64 of 200 splits. On the controlled matrix, Fable 5.1 has 445 of 864 attempts accepted, Astra 6 422, Opus 5.5 405, and Sol 5.6 385 (p=0.001p=0.001); the split-half τ\tau is 0.80 (p=0.001p=0.001), and the halves give the same order in 102 of 200 splits. On the PPA track, Fable 5.1 improves 184 of 384 designs and Sol 5.6 151, against 123 and 111 for Astra 6 and Opus 5.5 (p<0.001p<0.001); the split-half τ\tau is 0.87 (p=0.001p=0.001), and the halves give the same order in 116 of 200 splits. Each ranking describes its own experiment: Sol 5.6 is first on the correctness track, second on the PPA track, and last on the controlled matrix. The overall score of Appendix D.9 combines the two tracks of the benchmark and leaves the diagnostic studies out.

On the controlled matrix, Sol 5.6 falls behind through designs it submits and the grader rejects. At 16 steps, each agent ends 93 to 96 of its 216 attempts at a cap. Sol 5.6 has 63 of its 121 submitted designs rejected, against 54 of 121 for Opus 5.5, 48 of 120 for Astra 6, and 35 of 123 for Fable 5.1. Of Sol 5.6’s 63, 50 were submitted while failing public tests the agent had seen (24 of 35 for Fable 5.1), and the grader’s primary diagnosis is arithmetic for 28, integration for 22, and state or protocol for 13. Its rejected submissions grow from 24 at one step to 63 at 16, against 18 and 35 for Fable 5.1, and at 16 steps it has 21 and 37 attempts accepted at the 1×\times and 1.5×\times budgets, against 37 and 50 for Fable 5.1. On the six scaffold-adaptation tasks of the correctness track, Sol 5.6 submits 196 of 232 attempts, more than any other agent, and 18 of those submissions fail the public tests it had seen, the fewest of the four.

On the correctness track, three pairwise differences are distinguishable from zero after a Holm adjustment over the six pairs (Table 52): Sol 5.6 over Astra 6, 11.4 points with a 95% interval of 6.4 to 16.5; Sol 5.6 over Fable 5.1, 12.9 points (8.1 to 18.0); and Opus 5.5 over Fable 5.1, 7.6 points (2.5 to 12.7). All four agents are accepted on 99 of the 472 instances and none on 74; on the other 299, the agents disagree. Any two agents disagree on about 35% of the instances, so at this size the track detects a paired difference of about 8 points with 80% power. Among the twelve tasks, three separate the agents after a Holm adjustment: Gemma 3 4B from interfaces (p<0.001p<0.001), where Astra 6 and Fable 5.1 are accepted on 9 and 14 of 64 instances against 28 and 31 for Opus 5.5 and Sol 5.6; scaffold adaptation of Llama 3.2-1B (p=0.007p=0.007), where Sol 5.6 is accepted on 54 of 64 instances and the others on 35 to 41; and scaffold adaptation of Qwen3.5-4B (p=0.015p=0.015), where Opus 5.5 is accepted on 12 of 24 instances and the others on 20 or 21.

D.9 Overall score

The overall score of Section 2.4 multiplies a correctness-track score by a PPA-track score. The correctness score is the acceptance rate on each of the twelve correctness-track tasks, averaged over the tasks, so the tasks with 64 instances weigh no more than those with 24. The PPA score is the rate of improved designs on each of Qwen3.5-0.8B and 4B, Gemma 4 E4B, and Llama 3.2 3B, averaged over the four. Table 53 gives the score, its two factors, and the other rates of both tracks. Intervals are paired percentile bootstraps: each resample draws instances with replacement within each task and keeps the four agents’ outcomes on an instance together.

Fable 5.1 and Sol 5.6 score 25.0 and 24.5, and Astra 6 and Opus 5.5 score 16.8 and 16.5. The four differences between an agent of the first pair and one of the second are 7.7 to 8.5 points (Table 54). The bootstrap intervals of all four exclude zero, and a paired permutation test gives a Holm-adjusted pp of 0.002 for each. Within each pair the difference is 0.5 and 0.3 points, and Fable 5.1 has the highest score in 58% of the resamples against 42% for Sol 5.6. We also test whether the ranking reproduces (Table 56). Each split divides the matched instances of every correctness task and PPA target into two random halves and computes the score on each half. Both halves rank Sol 5.6 and Fable 5.1 above Astra 6 and Opus 5.5 in all 200 splits, against 17% of splits when the four agents’ outcomes are permuted within instances (p=0.001p=0.001).

Which of the first two agents leads depends on how the tracks are combined (Table 55). Sol 5.6 has the higher correctness score and Fable 5.1 the higher PPA score. Fable 5.1 is first under the product, and Sol 5.6 under the mean of the two track scores and when the sixteen tasks weigh equally, which gives the PPA track one quarter of the weight. Under every definition that includes the PPA track, both score above Astra 6 and Opus 5.5. We multiply the track scores because the benchmark asks for a design that is both correct and efficient: the product is high only when both rates are, and it is the probability that one attempt at a randomly drawn correctness task and one at a randomly drawn PPA target both succeed, if the two are independent.

Applying Equation 3 at the clock each design achieves after place and route changes 107 of the 1,536 labels and gives scores of 23.7 for Sol 5.6, 22.8 for Fable 5.1, 14.9 for Astra 6, and 15.6 for Opus 5.5 (Table 65); each of the four differences between an agent of the first pair and one of the second has a Holm-adjusted pp of at most 0.002.

Appendix E PPA track and backend

E.1 Power methodology and reference schedules

Table 57 compares the baseline and optimized schedules of the Qwen3.5-0.8B and 4B reference designs before place and route.

Paired comparison.

Both optimized schedules raise throughput by 12.0% and add about 300 LUTs (under 1%) in the pre-route estimate. After place and route (Appendix E.2), the optimized designs use 61.5k (0.8B) and 69.2k (4B) LUTs, against the estimated 62.1k and 69.3k. Both designs time-multiplex a shared compute engine and stream weights from external storage, so the larger model adds computation and memory traffic without a proportionally larger datapath. Within each workload, the two schedules use the same arithmetic and therefore have the same fidelity.

The optimized schedules raise FPGA-plus-DRAM power by about 3.9%, so the 12.0% throughput gain gives an estimated efficiency gain of 7.8%. Energy per token falls from 2.2456 to 2.0831 J (Qwen3.5-0.8B) and from 12.6125 to 11.6964 J (Qwen3.5-4B).

Evidence levels.

We report power at three levels: estimates, post-route reports, and board measurements. Estimates come from a power budget, which links power and work counts to energy, or from a post-synthesis power report, which assumes a clock, voltage, temperature, process, and switching activity. Post-route reports add physical implementation information, and board measurements observe the running design (Appendix E.2). Vendor guidance [AMD, 2026a] emphasizes both switching annotation and implementation information.

Sensitivity.

Let gR=R1/R0g_{R}=R_{1}/R_{0} and gP=P1/P0g_{P}=P_{1}/P_{0}. The energy-efficiency gain is gR/gP−1g_{R}/g_{P}-1, so it vanishes when power rises as much as throughput: the 10.5% throughput gain for Qwen3.5-nano gives no energy benefit if power also rises by 10.5%, and the 12.0% gains for 0.8B and 4B break even at a 12.0% power increase.

E.2 Physical implementation and board power

The baseline and optimized schedules of the 0.8B and 4B reference designs were each placed and routed with three implementation seeds and measured on the board with five repeats per seed (Figure 21, Tables 60 and 61). Every baseline implementation and every optimized 4B implementation meets 126 MHz. The optimized 0.8B design meets it on one of three seeds; the other two close at a lower clock, so its mean operating clock is 125.3 MHz and its throughput gain is 11.4–11.8%. Mean post-route LUT counts change by −0.2-0.2% for both workloads, where the estimates of Table 57 showed an increase of about 300 LUTs, and BRAM rises by 2.2% and 1.6%.

Measured board power rises by 3.1% (0.8B) and 3.7% (4B), and energy per token falls by 7.8% and 7.1%. The resulting efficiency gains, 8.5% and 7.7%, lie within a percentage point of the estimated 7.8%. Paired by seed and repeat, all 15 board pairs of each workload show an efficiency gain, from 3.5% to 13.6% for 0.8B and from 4.7% to 12.4% for 4B, with seed means of 7.5–9.3% and 6.9–8.2%. All implementations target the AMD Alveo U250 device xcu250-figd2104-2L-e and were built with Vivado 2024.1, the version recorded in the Vivado logs, timing reports, and bitstream headers. Board power is read from the U250’s on-board sensors through XRT 2.16.204 and sums the core (0.85 V), auxiliary (1.8 V), and DRAM (1.2 V) rails, sampled at 1 kHz. Each seed is measured in five non-overlapping 10 s windows. The reported board power is the total of the three rails during these windows, the same quantity as the post-route estimates it is compared with; each rail’s median idle power over the 30 s before the workload is recorded and is not subtracted. The memory-service model is cycle-relative: a request waits 48 cycles, each 64-byte beat then takes one cycle, bursts have 8 to 16 beats, and the interface delivers at most one beat per cycle at 126 MHz; under the bounded-memory-stall condition of the regrading and the controlled matrix, response delays are drawn uniformly from 0 to 256 cycles. The held-out backpressure test and the local checks use shorter stalls of one to three cycles (Appendix B.1).

Further references and agent designs.

The nano, Gemma 4 E4B, and Llama 3.2 3B references were placed and routed with three seeds each and measured on the board with five windows per seed (Table 58). All operate at 126 MHz. Gemma 4 E4B decodes 0.940 tokens/s with 73.6k LUTs and an estimated 10.61 W, Llama 3.2 3B 1.120 tokens/s with 67.1k LUTs and 10.07 W, and nano 365.12 tokens/s with 46.8k LUTs and 5.92 W; the nano rate comes from a single prepared transaction. The Gemma 3 4B and Llama 3.2-1B references were placed and routed with three seeds each and close timing at 126 MHz on every seed: Gemma 3 4B decodes 0.883 tokens/s with 73.5k LUTs and an estimated 10.55 W, and Llama 3.2-1B 2.961 tokens/s with 60.4k LUTs and 8.99 W. One improved PPA design per agent on each Qwen3.5 target, the one with the largest nominal gain, was also measured on the board, with three seeds and five windows each. Across these eight designs and the three references, mean board power differs from the post-route activity estimate by −0.62-0.62 to +3.47+3.47%, and seed means by −1.70-1.70 to +4.21+4.21% (Table 59, Figure 20).

FPGA and ASIC implementation flows.

Every physical result in this paper comes from the FPGA flow described above. Vivado implementation places a synthesized netlist onto the U250’s existing resources (look-up tables, flip-flops, block RAM, DSP slices, and programmable interconnect), routes it, checks timing, and writes a bitstream [AMD, 2026b]. The quantities it yields are resource counts, the clock the routed design achieves, and, on the board, rail power. OpenROAD [Ajayi et al., 2019] and the flows built on it target ASIC design: starting from RTL and a process design kit, they synthesize to a standard-cell library and carry the design through floorplanning, macro and standard-cell placement, clock-tree synthesis, global and detailed routing, and layout generation in GDSII. Their outputs are a cell area, routed timing, congestion, and power for a chip that would be fabricated, with design-rule checks before signoff. The two flows therefore answer different questions about the same RTL. The contract, the oracle, and the simulation-based tests are independent of the implementation flow; the PPA criterion of Equation 3 is stated in FPGA LUTs at a 126 MHz clock. Extending the PPA track to ASICs would require choosing a PDK and standard-cell library, generating or selecting memory macros for the caches and weight buffers, writing timing constraints for that process, adding physical verification, and restating the area term in cell area. Such results would not be comparable with the LUT counts and board power reported here.

E.3 Schedule mechanisms and operating conditions

A cycle model shows where the optimized schedule saves time. For both workloads, compute, memory waits, and control take 65, 28, and 7% of the cycles per token under the baseline schedule and 73, 22, and 5% under the optimized one. Doubling memory bandwidth raises the Qwen3.5-0.8B baseline throughput by 14%, from 3.999 to 4.563 tokens/s. In the cycle and power model for Qwen3.5-4B, enabling buffering, overlap, and the revised schedule together lowers cycles per token by 10.7%, and overlap gives the largest single reduction. In sweeps that vary bandwidth, latency, prompt length, or resource budget one at a time around the nominal operating point, the optimized schedule keeps its advantage, and its relative gain is largest when memory latency is high or bandwidth is low.

E.4 PPA track: agent optimization

Starting from the correct reference design of Qwen3.5-0.8B, Qwen3.5-4B, Gemma 4 E4B, or Llama 3.2 3B, agents try to improve throughput, resources, or energy efficiency while keeping the design correct (Figure 22, Table 62). Each agent makes 96 attempts per target. Of the 1,536 attempts, 965 keep the design correct and 569 also meet Equation 3, where R0R_{0} and L0L_{0} are the throughput and LUT count of the starting design: for 0.8B and 4B the baseline of Table 57 (3.999 and 0.800 tokens/s, 61.8k and 69.0k LUTs), and for Gemma 4 E4B and Llama 3.2 3B the evaluator’s values for their reference designs (0.940 and 1.120 tokens/s, 74.4k and 66.6k LUTs). Recomputing the three gains from the measured throughput, LUT, and energy values and applying Equation 3 to each attempt reproduces all 1,536 labels.

Per agent and target, between 18 of 96 (Opus 5.5, 0.8B) and 55 of 96 (Fable 5.1, 4B) attempts are improved, at 20.7 to 51.8 agent-hours per improved design. Among the 569 improved designs, the median throughput gain per target is 14.2 to 14.5%, the median efficiency gain 10.9 to 11.2%, and the median LUT change −1.1-1.1 to −0.7-0.7%. Because the criterion caps LUT growth, this subset is selected partly on LUT change; over all 965 correct submissions, median gains are smaller and LUT use rises slightly (Table 63). The other 571 attempts end without a correct design, from 90 of 384 for Fable 5.1 to 185 of 384 for Astra 6 (Table 49). Of these, 194 submit an incorrect design, and 377 reach a cap (207 on wall time, 88 on tool calls, and 82 on output tokens) with RTL that fails the correctness checks. Because every attempt here starts from the same correct design, these gains can be compared across agents, unlike the throughput and LUT counts of accepted correctness-track designs in Appendix G.

Place and route of agent designs.

Each of the 965 correct designs was placed and routed with three implementation seeds, 2,895 runs in all: 2,855 complete, 27 fail to route, and 13 time out, so 925 designs complete all three (Figure 23, Table 64). After routing, a design counts as improved when it is correct, all three routes complete, its mean throughput at the achieved clock is at least 1.05 times the starting design’s, and its mean LUT count is at most 1.02 times the baseline at the same stage. Of the 1,536 attempts, 528 meet this rule, against 569 at the nominal clock: 495 keep the label, 74 lose it, and 33 gain it. Fable 5.1 loses the most labels, 28, which leaves it 168 routed improvements against 184 nominal; Sol 5.6 has 146, Astra 6 109, and Opus 5.5 105. Among routed improvements, the median throughput gain per agent and target is 9.7 to 20.0% and the median LUT change −3.8-3.8 to +0.3+0.3%. Timing closure at 126 MHz is recorded separately; per agent and target, 65 to 87% of the route runs close it. Table 65 recomputes the overall score with the routed labels; the correctness factor is unchanged.

Appendix F Reference designs across decoder families

F.1 Configurations and detailed checks for additional decoders

The four additional reference designs of Sections 2.3 and 3.3 (Table 4) are for Gemma 2 2B [Google, 2024] (google/gemma-2-2b), the text decoder of Gemma 3 4B [Google DeepMind, 2025] (google/gemma-3-4b-it), Qwen3.6-27B, and Llama 3.2-1B. Image processing is excluded from the Gemma 3 task. For the three attention-only targets, the GDN and convolution components of sts_{t} in Equation 1 are empty.

The Gemma 2 2B public suite, like the suites of the earlier eight-step Gemma 3 4B and Llama 3.2-1B runs (Appendix D.2), has 1,000 cases on primitive operators, 128 on an attention layer, 128 on a complete decoder block, 32 on one-step model execution, 16 on eight-step decoding, and 16 on reset/isolation. Its held-out suite has 16 cases each on new token prefixes, supported nonzero cache positions, reset after activity, bounded in-order stalls, and shape-compatible parameter reload. The 32-step suites of the Gemma 3 4B and Llama 3.2-1B tasks have 1,024 operator cases, 192 on individual layers, 192 on a complete decoder block, 64 on one-step execution, 64 on 32-step decoding, and 64 on reset isolation, 1,600 in all, and 48 held-out cases in each of the same five families, 240 in all.

On common prefixes, the Gemma 2 2B contract matches FP32 on 1,574 of 1,600 top-1 decisions and the Gemma 3 4B contract on 1,584 (Table 67 gives the percentages by position). Gemma 2 2B therefore misses the 99% fidelity threshold although its RTL matches its integer oracle on every case. Building these reference designs involved no agent attempts.

Qwen3.6-27B and Llama 3.2-1B.

The Qwen3.6-27B configuration [Qwen Team, 2026b] is a dense hybrid decoder with 64 layers, hidden width 5,120, and a full-attention layer every fourth layer. Like the Qwen3.5 configurations [Qwen Team, 2026a, Qwen Team, 2026c], it has a gated attention output, but reusing the Qwen3.5 scaffold still required checking gate arithmetic, state layouts, and address ranges. Its public suite has 1,000 operator cases, 128 GDN-layer cases, 128 full-attention-layer cases, 32 one-step cases, 16 eight-step cases, and 16 reset cases. All operator and layer cases pass, but four one-step and four eight-step cases fail. Table 66 gives its ten held-out failures by condition.

Llama 3.2-1B [Meta, 2024] is a compact text-only decoder from a third family. Its suites have the same allocation as the Gemma 3 4B suites, under its own attention, normalization, and positional contract, and all 1,600 public and 240 held-out cases of its 32-step suite pass.

Table 67 gives fidelity by position for the four additional targets, with 200 decisions at each of eight positions. Pooled top-1 agreement is 1,574 of 1,600 for Gemma 2 2B, 1,584 for Gemma 3 4B, 1,584 for Qwen3.6-27B, and 1,589 for Llama 3.2-1B. Only Gemma 2 2B falls below the 99% fidelity threshold. Qwen3.6-27B’s RTL matches its integer oracle on 1,312 of 1,320 public and 70 of 80 held-out cases, Gemma 2 2B’s on all 1,400 cases of its suites, and Gemma 3 4B’s and Llama 3.2-1B’s on all 1,840 of theirs (Table 4).

F.1.1 Validation levels

The pooled case counts in Table 4 weight every test case equally, but most public cases exercise operators and layers. By level, Gemma 2 2B, Gemma 3 4B, and Llama 3.2-1B pass every level. Qwen3.6-27B passes 1,312 of 1,320 public cases overall: all 1,256 operator and single-layer cases, but only 28/32 (87.5%) of the one-step cases and 12/16 (75.0%) of the eight-step cases.

Table 66 breaks the held-out cases down by condition. Qwen3.6-27B’s failures span several conditions: four of 16 cases fail under bounded stalls, three at supported cache positions, two on new prefixes, and one on idle parameter reload, while all 16 reset-after-activity cases pass. The other three targets pass all five conditions under their own contracts.

F.1.2 Fidelity by position

Table 67 breaks the pooled fidelity of all six targets into eight decode positions. Qwen3.5-0.8B meets the threshold on the pooled score but falls below 99% at positions 3 and 6, whereas Qwen3.5-4B stays at or above 99% at every position. Gemma 3 4B and Qwen3.6-27B both pool to exactly 99%, with three and two positions below it, and Llama 3.2-1B’s pooled 99.31% includes 98.0% at position 3. Gemma 2 2B has the lowest pooled fidelity, with four positions below 99% and a minimum of 97.5%, although its RTL is exact on every case.

F.2 Qwen3.6-27B repairs and Gemma 2 2B precision

Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma 2 2B do not qualify, for different reasons (Section 3.3). We revised the Qwen3.6-27B RTL twice and evaluated eight alternative integer contracts for Gemma 2 2B.

The two revisions of the Qwen3.6-27B reference reduce its failures from eighteen cases, all at the integration levels (Appendix F.1.1), to one or two (Figure 24a, Table 68). Revision A passes all 80 held-out cases but misses one eight-step public case and one regression case under stalls. Revision B passes every public and regression case but misses one held-out parameter-reload case. Neither revision passes every check, so Qwen3.6-27B does not qualify.

Gemma 2 2B’s fidelity shortfall is a property of its contract: seven of eight alternative integer contracts reach the 99% fidelity threshold, from 99.12% with 8-bit calibrated per-channel scaling to 99.90% at 16 bits (Table 69). Higher precision costs hardware: LUT counts rise from 58.4k to 84.1k, and throughput falls from 1.48 to 0.90 tokens/s. All four additional reference designs meet timing, and Gemma 3 4B and Llama 3.2-1B pass every gate (Table 70).

Appendix G Earlier task series

Before the runs of the correctness track, the four agents ran an earlier series of four tasks under full-state feedback: Qwen3.5-nano T1 (one decoder layer), T2 (the four-layer decoder for one step), and T3 (eight recurrent steps), each built from interfaces with 16 attempts per agent, and scaffold adaptation of Qwen3.5-0.8B with 12 attempts per agent (Table 71). The nano tasks follow the order in which a decoder accelerator is assembled, so each task requires more integration than the one before. Wall-time caps and test suites also grow from T1 to T3, so a difference between T1 and T3 combines integration, horizon, budget, and suite size. Sol 5.6 and Astra 6 ran these tasks first, on shared task instances, for 96 nano attempts and 24 adaptation attempts. A feedback pilot added 32 output-only Sol 5.6 attempts on T2 and T3, which gives the 152 attempts of this cohort. Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 ran the four tasks later with the same harness, caps, test counts, and feedback. Because the two cohorts ran at different times, we compare agents only within a cohort.

Acceptance.

Every agent has fewer attempts accepted on the recurrent decoder (T3) than on the single layer (T1) (Table 72): by 50.0 and 31.3 percentage points for Sol 5.6 and Astra 6, and by 12.5 and 6.3 points for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5. Pooled over the four agents, acceptance is similar on T1 and T2 (46/64 and 43/64) and falls to 30/64 on T3. The controlled matrix (Appendix D.5) varies the horizon from one starting implementation. On Qwen3.5-0.8B, 7 to 11 of each agent’s 12 attempts are accepted. This task measures adaptation of a common parameterized scaffold.

Passing the public suite overstates acceptance in both cohorts. Nine Sol 5.6 and nine Astra 6 submissions pass it and fail final acceptance, 16 of the 18 on the held-out suite, as do six Opus 5.5 submissions (three diagnosed as integration, two as state/protocol, and one as arithmetic) and one Fable 5.1 submission (arithmetic). Lower acceptance and longer attempts also compound in cost: from T1 to T3, agent-hours per accepted design grow from 2.32 to 15.14 for Sol 5.6 and from 2.48 to 10.09 for Astra 6, and Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 need 7.39 and 5.96 on T3.

Feedback pilot.

Sol 5.6 attempted 16 instances each of T2 and T3 under output-only feedback, paired with its full-state attempts on the same instances. Full-state feedback adds two accepted attempts per task, from 8 to 10 of 16 on T2 and from 3 to 5 of 16 on T3, with four discordant pairs each (exact McNemar p=0.625p=0.625). The feedback study of Appendix D.4 repeats the comparison with four agents and 32 instances per task. Listing 2 gives the record of one output-only T3 attempt that passes the public checks visible to the agent and fails the recheck after submission. In the record, visible_public counts the public checks the agent saw, canonical_public the state-aware public recheck, and hidden_numerical the held-out suite.

Hardware of accepted designs.

Throughput is the 126 MHz target clock divided by elapsed cycles per token, at batch size one and an eight-token prompt under the common memory-service model. For the seven accepted Sol 5.6 designs and the eight accepted Astra 6 designs on Qwen3.5-0.8B, median decode throughput is 4.398 and 4.337 tokens/s, with ranges of 4.240–4.494 and 4.225–4.527 tokens/s; median mapped LUT counts are 61,995 and 61,910 (Table 73). Sol 5.6 has the higher median throughput, but the two nondominated designs in the throughput–LUT plane are both Astra 6 submissions, at (61,325 LUTs, 4.392 tokens/s) and (61,680 LUTs, 4.527 tokens/s). The PPA track compares the agents’ optimization from a common correct design (Appendix E.4).
